transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you. Well... I guess what brings me in is that I keep getting these awful doubts that I've missed something important. 

It happens with all sorts of things, really. It could be a number on the mortgage payment, a small detail in a client proof for work, or even just a door not being latched. And the frustrating part is, even when I know I checked it, the thought just barges right back into my head. It's always this nagging feeling of, you know, "What if this is the mistake that costs you everything?" It's just become very exhausting to deal with.

When you get these doubts and worries, do you find yourself doing things repeatedly to try to relieve the anxiety—like checking the door multiple times, recounting numbers, or reviewing your work over and over?

Yes, that's exactly what I do. I'll... well, I end up reopening my design files, or rereading emails over and over. If it's a bill, I keep going back and checking the online payment confirmation. Sometimes I even just say the figures silently in my head, repeating them until things finally feel... settled, I guess. 

It's really becoming a problem for my work. A simple invoice or just a basic logo revision can turn into hours of checking, and those are hours I obviously can't bill a client for.

When you repeat those figures silently in your head or say them until things feel settled—is that the main way you try to calm the anxiety, or do you find yourself also doing physical actions like writing things down, arranging things, or physically checking things multiple times?

Well, it's mostly the mental checking and repeating, like I mentioned. I mean, I do physically check the door or look at the computer screen multiple times, but I don't really write things down or arrange objects to calm down. It's more about going over the information again and again, either by looking at it or repeating it in my head, until that awful feeling of doubt finally goes away.

When you're doing all this checking and repeating, do you recognize at that moment that these thoughts might be excessive or that the checking probably isn't really necessary—or does it feel completely justified and necessary to you?

I... well, I'm not entirely sure how to answer that. I guess logically, I know it's excessive. Like, I know I shouldn't need to check a simple invoice five or six times. But when I'm actually in the middle of it, the doubt is just so strong that the checking feels completely necessary. 

It feels like if I don't do it, something terrible will slip through. It's really only afterward, when I realize how much time I've lost, that I can clearly see how unnecessary it all was. But in the moment? It just feels like something I absolutely have to do.

If I told you right now that you absolutely do not need to check that invoice again, and that nothing bad will happen if you skip the checking—do you think you could believe that and stop yourself, or would the doubt and urge to check still feel overwhelming?

I don't think I could just stop. Even if you told me that, the urge would still be there. I might try to hold off for a minute, but the anxiety would just build and build until I'd have to go back and check it anyway. The doubt is just too strong to ignore, no matter what someone else says.

When you're in the middle of checking and repeating, and you're feeling that strong urge—do you actually believe that something bad really will happen if you don't check, or do you know deep down that it probably won't but the fear just feels too strong to resist?

I think... deep down, I know it probably won't happen. Like, logically, I know making a mistake on a design file or an invoice isn't going to cause some catastrophic disaster. But the fear just takes over. It feels so real in that moment, and the anxiety gets so intense that I just can't resist the urge to check. It's like my brain won't let me move on until I do it, even though a part of me knows it's irrational.
